column6: Confirmed: Bank Call Reports publicly disclose loan modification activity. Schedule RC-C, Part I Memorandum item 1 reports the total loans restructured (modified) that are current. Schedule RC-N (Past Due & Nonaccrual) Memorandum item 1 explicitly captures loans modified for financial difficulty that are delinquent or nonaccrualfdic.gov. In other words, all TDR-style modifications are recorded either in RC-C (performing) or RC-N (nonperforming), with breakdowns by loan type. All federal bank Call Reports (FFIEC 031/041) are available on the FFIEC website for each bank.
column7: This confirms the log’s assertion: anyone can download RC-C and RC-N for banks and compute the extent of loan modifications. By comparing these figures quarter-to-quarter, analysts can uncover whether banks are quietly extending loans. The availability of this data ties directly to credit risk surveillance. For example, a surge in RC-N “loan mods” versus RC-C “loan mods” would indicate rising hidden delinquencies. Thus, this reinforces that loan modification trends (especially when abnormal) are a direct leading indicator of stress in bank portfolios.

column6: FERRIS WHEEL RULE ACTIVE 12-month reporting window allows banks to hide cumulative modification exposure
column7: Track banks implementing early Q3 2025, monitor for false improvement narratives

column6: The FDIC finalized the so-called “Ferris Wheel” reporting window in mid-2025: banks must treat a loan as “modified” for 12 months post-modificationfdic.gov. This rule (effective for Q4 2025 data, optional Q3 2025 early) formalizes that every loan restructured for a borrower in difficulty remains flagged as modified for a year. After 12 months, if still nonperforming, it falls off that schedule.
column7: This change institutionalizes the prior practice of short-term rollovers. It means that cumulative exposure isn’t visible beyond a year: a loan modified 11 months ago appears identical on paper to a new loan mod, making trending tricky. This perpetuates the risk of complacency: bank executives can point to improved quarterly stats even though total problem loans have just been “spun” to a new window. It underscores the need to track aggregate volumes of 12-month “cycles” of modified loans. In effect, it links to systemic risk by giving banks room to manage the optics of delinquencies, reinforcing the log’s concern about false improvement narratives.
